Regions are urged to cut arms on their own doorstep in Resolution A/69/45, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The vote stands in a chain that reaches back to 1990. Its faith is stated at the start. The drive of states toward full disarmament grows from a plain human wish. That wish is for true peace and safety, and for an end to the threat of war.

Peace kept in one region, the text argues, frees funds, minds, and goods for peaceful work. The call asks states to take up regional arms steps that fit their own ground. Trust built near home, in this view, is the base on which wider arms deals can stand.
un-ga-res-45:
Food stayed short long after the guns fell silent, and Resolution 45 of the General Assembly, passed on 11 December 1946, takes stock of the crisis. In February the Assembly had urged swift action on a feared lack of bread grains and rice. By year's end, the joint effort had paid off. The grain state of 1946 was far better than feared. Millions of lives had been saved in the hard months before harvest.

Yet the text warns that the food state stays poor. Many lands had not yet shaken off the ruin of enemy rule and still needed forced imports of grains, fats, and other staples. A sharp lack of such foods held on in much of Europe, even in lands that once sold food abroad.

It rests on the Secretary-General's first report on how Resolution 143 was being carried out. The Council calls on Belgium to carry out the withdrawal of its troops quickly, and it authorizes the Secretary-General to take all action needed for that end. It asks all states to avoid any act that could block the return of law and order or weaken the Congolese government's authority. The Congo operation was becoming a test of what UN forces could do.

Jadranka Rota and David Wagner described a role reversal in nature in a 2006 PLOS ONE paper. Metalmark moths, small butterflies' cousins, are prey for jumping spiders. Yet these moths mimic those very spiders, their own predators. Mimicry usually means copying something dangerous to scare hunters off; copying the hunter itself is a rarer trick.

The moths' posture and markings echo a jumping spider closely enough to matter. A spider that hesitates, mistaking prey for a rival or a threat, gives the moth its chance to escape. The study documents the disguise and weighs how it works, adding a strange and tidy case to the science of animal deception.
luther-bible-1545:
Martin Luther's German Bible appeared in its final form in 1545, printed by Hans Lufft at Wittenberg. Its title promises the whole Holy Scripture in German, newly prepared. Luther had worked on the translation for over twenty years, and the 1545 printing was the last edition he oversaw himself before his death.

The text is the complete Bible in Early New High German. Luther chose words ordinary people spoke, and that choice helped fix a shared written German across many small states. The book also shows his own notes and revisions from a lifetime of preaching. It stayed the standard German Bible for centuries.
gregory-great-morals-on-job-vol-2-1845:
Volume two of Gregory the Great's Morals on the Book of Job appeared in 1845, in the Rev. James Bliss translation for the Library of the Fathers. It holds Parts Three and Four of the Moralia, the commentary Gregory wrote in the late 500s on the Bible's great book about suffering.

arxiv-2606-05145: When an AI's chain of thought goes wrong, reading the trace rarely reveals how to fix it. arxiv-2606-05245: The Preisach model captures hysteresis — systems that remember their history, like magnets — and its extremum stack is the data structure tracking that memory. arxiv-2606-05345: Transformers need to know the order of words, and relative attention schemes encode positions cleverly. arxiv-2606-05745: Quantum channels — the noisy processes transforming quantum states — are hard to characterize exactly. arxiv-2606-05845: Fluctuational electrodynamics describes heat carried by electromagnetic fluctuations — dominant when objects nearly touch. tob-13145:
Swami Vivekananda crossed the world in the 1890s to teach Hindu thought to Western audiences. Seven of his lectures on Jnana Yoga, the path of knowledge, form Part Two of that course. Vivekananda was trained in Advaita Vedanta, the teaching that the self and the divine are one.

Lecture by lecture he argues that the soul is already divine and that fear and weakness come from forgetting it. Reason, he says, pushed honestly to its end, leads past itself into direct realization. His forceful, plain speech made abstract doctrine feel urgent. The lectures helped plant Indian philosophy firmly in the West.
tob-0045:
Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara ordered a private history of how the United States slid into the Vietnam War. The study, leaked in 1971, became famous as the Pentagon Papers. Volume one of the edition entered into the record by Senator Mike Gravel covers the years from Truman through Johnson.

Inside, memos and cables show leaders doubting the war in private while pressing it in public. The leak fed a landmark fight over press freedom and helped turn opinion against the war. Gravel's edition put the documents themselves before ordinary readers. The volume remains the paper trail behind the headlines of a generation.
tob-4145:
Julius Jolly translated the Vishnu Smriti for volume seven of the Sacred Books of the East in 1882. The Hindu law-book speaks in Vishnu's name and orders life by dharma. It sets the duties of the four castes and the stages of a man's life. It also gives penances for faults, and rules of gift and purity.

Kings learn how to judge cases and set punishments. Householders learn debts, inheritance, and the rites owed to ancestors. Jolly, a fine scholar of Indian law, keeps the dense rules clear. Verified from the 1919 edition, the Smriti shows ancient India's legal mind at work on daily life.
tob-4245:
Arthur Middleton Reeves weighed the evidence for Norse America in The Finding of Wineland the Good, published in 1890. His subject is the Icelandic sagas of voyages west: Bjarni's sighting, Leif Eriksson's landing, and the farms raised in a land of vines and timber. Reeves, an American scholar of Icelandic, sorts saga from saga.

He compares the accounts, maps the likely coasts, and judges what the tales can prove. Five centuries before Columbus, on his showing, Norsemen wintered in the New World. Verified from the 1919 edition, the study remains a careful, readable brief for the Vinland voyages and their sources.
darwin-voyage-beagle-murray-1845:
Charles Darwin's Journal of Researches, better known as the Voyage of the Beagle, tells the 1831 to 1836 circumnavigation that made him a scientist. The text here is the second edition of 1845, published by John Murray, which Darwin revised and expanded. He sailed as the ship's naturalist, unpaid, at age twenty-two.

The journal moves from Brazil's forests to Patagonia's fossil beds, the Andes, and the Galapagos. Darwin describes giant extinct mammals, mockingbirds that differ by island, and coral atolls sinking into lagoons. His eye for pattern turns travel notes into quiet revolutions. The observations seeded the Origin of Species fourteen years later. The book itself is one of the great travel works in English.
lawes-against-witches-1645:
The Lawes against Witches and Coniuration, printed in 1645, is not a tale but a tool. It sets out the statutes that made witchcraft a crime punishable by death. The year matters: 1645 was the height of Matthew Hopkins's witch hunt in East Anglia.

Hopkins, who styled himself Witchfinder General, worked the courts of Essex, Suffolk, and beyond. His teams used these laws to send scores of people to trial and many to the gallows. The pamphlet gave justices, jurors, and readers the exact words of the law. It is the legal spine of England's worst witch panic.
williford-cariden-examination-1645:
Joane Williford and Joan Cariden of Kent went through charge, trial, and death in 1645, and a pamphlet keeps each stage. The Examination, Confession, Triall, and Execution prints the whole course of their case. The year places them in the Hopkins panic, when eastern courts sat full of such work.

Readers get the first questions, the words taken as confession, the verdict, and the end. Few prints hold all four stages of a witch case in so small a space. The record shows the speed with which a life could pass through the machine of the law. It is grim, plain, and complete.
quicherat-proces-jeanne-darc-vol3-1845:
Witnesses carry Quicherat's third volume, printed in 1845. It holds the testimony given in 1455 and 1456, when a new court re-tried Joan of Arc's name. Men and women who knew her spoke a full twenty-five years after her death.

Friends from her village, soldiers from her campaigns, and townsfolk from Orléans tell what they saw. Their words rebuild her early life, her battles, and her time in prison from the ground up. The inquiry cleared her name on the strength of this proof. The volume is the most human of the five, full of living voices.
ulrich-lanzelet-hahn-1845:
Ulrich von Zatzikhoven told the Lancelot story his own way in Lanzelet, a German poem of some 9,440 verses. Karl Hahn's 1845 edition prints the medieval text complete. His hero is raised far from court, by a fairy in a lake land.

Lanzelet grows up not knowing his own name or kin, then rides out to learn both by deeds. Tournaments, rescues, and strange hosts test him until he wins his place at the Round Table. The poem is an early, free branch of the Lancelot legend, apart from the French line. Hahn's edition keeps that branch within reach.
columella-de-re-rustica-english-1745:
Columella, a Roman Spaniard of the first century, wrote the most ordered ancient book on farming. Columella of Husbandry, in the English rendering of 1745, gives all twelve of his books. The 1745 version is the first complete Columella in English.

Book by book, he covers soils, grains, vines, trees, cattle, horses, poultry, bees, and the staff of a great estate. He writes as a working owner who has paced his own fields and barns. Roman farm craft stands at its fullest in these pages. English readers used this version as their Columella for two full centuries.
kerner-seeress-prevorst-1845:
Justinus Kerner tends a frail seer in The Seeress of Prevorst, in English from 1845. Kerner was a healer and poet in a small German town. His guest, Friederike Hauffe, lay ill for years, spoke in trance in strange tongues, drew rings of signs, and told of a world of souls in close touch with ours each day.

Kerner prints her words, draws, and cures with love and care. The book is part ward log, part hymn. It founds a whole kind of book: the seer as saint and case. Its glow still charms.
williford-examination-execution-1645:
Three Kent dames go to the gallows in the Examination pamphlet of 1645, a state tale from Faversham. Joan Williford, Joan Cariden, and Jane Hott were charged as witches in the year the great hunt gripped the east. The town's mayor took down their quiz, their words of guilt, their trial, and their deaths on September 29, all in one brief, grim print for the crowd to buy.

Such tales were oft loose and wild. This one is prim and full, which gives it rare worth. It is one day of a panic, kept whole. Its plain tone chills.
plaistow-poltergeist-1645:
Stones fly with no hand seen in Strange and Fearfull Newes from Plaistow, a brief tract of 1645. Plaistow was a hamlet by West Ham, then in the fields past London. In Paul Fox's house, stones and bricks flew round the rooms. E'en a sword flew, the tract says. Kin and guests watched in dread through days of the strange siege.

No witch is named, no cause is fixed in the text. It is a raw news cry, sold for a coin in the streets. Fans of ghost lore cite it as an early poltergeist tale.
reinaud-fave-feu-gregeois-1845:
Joseph Toussaint Reinaud and Ildefonse Fave wrote in French on Greek fire in 1845. Their book traces the lost fire weapon of Byzantium and the start of gunpowder. Greek fire could burn on water and sank many fleets. Its mix was a state secret for ages.

Old texts in Greek, Latin, and Arabic give the proof the pair work from. They tell how the fire was shot from tubes on ships and walls. Long notes weigh claims for the first use of powder in war. The book set the base for all later study of Greek fire.
poe-facts-case-m-valdemar-1845:
Edgar Allan Poe wrote The Facts in the Case of M. Valdemar in 1845. The tale is told as a true case from the mesmeric art. A man near death from lung rot grants a test of his friend's art. The friend holds him in a trance at the point of death.

Valdemar's tongue speaks from the trance: I am dead, it says, week by week. The flesh stays fresh while the voice begs for release at last. When the trance breaks, the corpse falls to rot in a flash. The tale was read as fact by some and is Poe's most grim art work.
poe-the-raven-1845:
Edgar Allan Poe published The Raven in 1845, and the poem made him famous at once. Many call it the most famous American poem of the nineteenth century in the world. Its music of loss and dread has been parodied and quoted ever since its debut.

A student, grieving his lost Lenore, sits at midnight in his chamber of books. A raven taps, enters, and perches on a bust of Pallas above his door. To each fond question the bird croaks one word, Nevermore, and will not leave. The student sinks from hope to despair as the refrain tolls like a bell. Poe's craft of sound and rhythm makes the short poem hard to forget.
dumas-twenty-years-after-1845:
Alexandre Dumas published Twenty Years After in 1845, the sequel to The Three Musketeers in France. The tale finds the four friends older, divided, and serving rival camps in civil war. Dumas set it in the Fronde and the English civil war of the 1640s there.

D'Artagnan, now a lieutenant, hunts his scattered friends for Cardinal Mazarin's service in secret missions. Athos guards the young Charles I's cause, while Aramis plots with the Fronde's princes in Paris. Milady's son Mordaunt stalks the four to avenge his mother's death at their hands years before. A daring bid to save Charles I from the scaffold gives the book its pathos. Age and loyalty, not youth, supply the sequel's deeper and graver pleasures in full.
dumas-marguerite-de-valois-1845:
Alexandre Dumas published Marguerite de Valois in 1845, first volume of his Wars of Religion trilogy. The great Valois romance turns on the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572 in Paris. Dumas blends court love and sectarian slaughter with his usual verve and speed of scene.

Marguerite weds Henri of Navarre to seal a peace between Catholic and Huguenot camps in France. Days later, the crown orders the massacre, and the Louvre runs with blood and terror. Lovers hide in closets, heads roll, and young Henri plays the fox to stay alive. Catherine de Medici schemes above all, with poison and astrology among her dark tools at court. The romance set the template for Dumas's later Valois sequels of court intrigue.
dumas-chevalier-de-maison-rouge-1845:
Alexandre Dumas published The Chevalier de Maison-Rouge in 1845, a romance of the French Terror. The tale follows the Chevalier de Rougeville's real plot to save Marie Antoinette in prison there. Many rank it the Terror's most thrilling adventure in the whole Dumas historical shelf in French.

Maurice Lindey, a young republican officer, loves Geneviève, wife of a royalist conspirator in Paris secretly. The Chevalier smuggles a file and a coded carnation into the queen's cell at the Temple. Plots fail by inches, and the queen goes to the scaffold as history records her fate. Maurice and his beloved choose the guillotine together rather than live apart in the Terror. Dumas wrings high romance from the Revolution's grimmest year without falsifying its end.
sarmiento-facundo-1845:
Domingo Faustino Sarmiento published Facundo in 1845, his great essay on Argentina's soul in the Rosas years. The life of the caudillo Facundo Quiroga becomes an argument about civilization and barbarism in the young republic. Sarmiento wrote it in Chilean exile, in haste, as a blow against the dictator Rosas and his gaucho armies.

Quiroga, a tiger of the plains, rises by horsemanship, terror, and a genius for the pampas' rough democracy of force. Sarmiento reads the land itself, its emptiness and distances, as the mother of caudillos and the enemy of cities. Biography, geography, and political pamphlet fuse in prose of famous energy, haste, and rhetorical fire. He dreams of schools, immigrants, and railways civilizing the desert that bred the men he fought in exile. The book founded Argentine letters and still frames its national argument about itself.
merimee-carmen-1845:
Prosper Merimee published Carmen in 1845, a French novella set in Spain. Don Jose is a soldier who falls under the spell of Carmen, a Romani woman who works in a cigarette factory in Seville. He helps her escape arrest, loses his rank, and joins smugglers. His obsession grows as her love cools.

Carmen values her freedom above any man's claim on her. The clash ends in murder, which the narrator recounts after meeting Jose in prison. Merimee writes in a cool, spare style that heightens the tragedy. The story later became Bizet's famous opera. The novella itself remains sharp and unsettling.
newman-essay-development-christian-doctr:
Newman wrote An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine in 1845, in the last months before he left the Church of England for Rome. The book asks how a faith can change over centuries and still stay itself. It became the theological bridge of his conversion, and of much modern Catholic thought.

Newman argues that a living idea grows, branching into new forms while keeping its first type and principles. He tests that claim against the early church, heresies, councils, and the slow growth of doctrine. His seven notes for telling true growth from corruption still get debated by theologians today.
fuller-woman-nineteenth-century-1845:
Margaret Fuller published Woman in the Nineteenth Century in 1845 in New York. Fuller, editor of The Dial and a leading figure among the Transcendentalists, expanded an earlier essay for the book. It became the founding text of American feminism in its full book form.

Fuller called for women's self-dependence: the freedom to think, learn, and act without asking leave of fathers or husbands. She surveyed myth, history, and marriage law to show how women had been stunted and what they might become. Her style is dense and allusive, her demand plain. Later suffragists built on her case. The book still reads as a brave, searching plea for women's intellectual equality.
livy-history-rome-books-37-45:
Books thirty-seven through forty-five close the surviving history of Livy, in the English version by D. Spillan and Cyrus Edmonds. Livy wrote under Augustus, and these last books run from 187 to 167 BCE. With them come the short summaries and fragments of the books that are lost.

Rome wars with Antiochus of Syria and takes Asia Minor, then crushes Macedon at Pydna and ends its kings. Livy keeps his eye on the senate, the triumphs, and the cost of empire at home. After book forty-five the grand narrative breaks off. What remains still crowns the fullest Roman account of the republic's rise to world rule.
zoist-vol-03-1845:
April 1845 to January 1846 is the span of The Zoist's third volume. Elliotson edits a journal now settled into its combative routine. Mesmeric surgery reports continue, each with witnesses and outcomes. Cerebral physiology, the era's study of brain and character, shares the pages.

Readers meet somnambulist cases that strain belief and invite tests. Country doctors write in with cures of pain, fits, and locked limbs. London critics answer, and the journal answers back. The thirteen volume run, from 1843 to 1856, holds the movement's whole record. Volume three is its sturdy middle beginning. It preserves a medical underground in its own words.
hahnemann-chronic-diseases-vol1-1845:
Hahnemann's second pillar beside the Organon is The Chronic Diseases, and Volume I reached English readers in Hempel's translation of 1845. Here Hahnemann sets out his psora doctrine, the claim that one deep taint underlies most long illness. The volume pairs that theory with the first of his antipsoric remedies.

Psora, in his telling, begins with the itch and spreads through the body over a lifetime. Cure means matching the case to a drug proved against that taint. The book changed homeopathic practice, turning many doctors toward deep, slow cases they once called incurable. Volume I lays the ground the other four build on.
hahnemann-chronic-diseases-vol2-1845:
Volume II of The Chronic Diseases, in the 1845 Hempel translation, moves from theory into the remedy records. Hahnemann's psora doctrine, his root-taint theory of long illness, fills the first volume. Here the antipsoric materia medica takes over, and drug follows drug in long, patient lists of proved symptoms.

These pages were working tools, meant to lie open on the desk during long and stubborn cases. Every line traces back to a proving, a test on a healthy person watched with care over days. Readers who work through the volume see Hahnemann's method at its most patient: observe, record, compare, then prescribe.
hahnemann-chronic-diseases-vol3-1845:
Psora theory gives Volume III of The Chronic Diseases its reason to exist, but the content is pure materia medica. In Hempel's 1845 English, Hahnemann's remedy records roll on in the same spare, steady style. A drug's signs appear in fixed order, from the mind through the whole body, section by section.

Chronic cases, Hahnemann taught, yield slowly and need remedies chosen for depth, not speed. The antipsoric drugs in these volumes were his chosen weapons against that deep taint. Doctors of his school kept the five volumes near the Organon itself, and Volume III holds the middle of that working library.
hahnemann-chronic-diseases-vol4-1845:
Volume IV of Hahnemann's Chronic Diseases, Englished by Hempel in 1845, nears the end of the antipsoric remedy list. The form stays plain: remedy after remedy, symptoms in their set order, no ornament. Behind each entry stand provings run under Hahnemann's own strict rules.

He demanded that provers note every change, however small, and these pages honor that demand. For modern readers the volume shows how homeopathy built its knowledge in its first age, one watched symptom at a time. As part of the five-volume whole it helped fix the psora doctrine in the school's mind.
hahnemann-chronic-diseases-vol5-1845:
With Volume V in 1845, the Hempel translation of The Chronic Diseases stands complete at last. Five volumes carry Hahnemann's late system: one root taint, psora, and a family of deep-acting remedies to meet it. The last volume rounds out the antipsoric materia medica and closes the remedy lists.

Taken with the Organon, the set forms the second pillar of classical homeopathy, as its readers have long called it. The symptom lists look dry, yet each line was a tool for matching a suffering patient to a single drug. Volume V closes an English edition that served the school for generations.
giorgi-de-harmonia-mundi-1545:
Francesco Giorgi sang the harmony of the whole world in De harmonia mundi totius, printed in 1545. The Franciscan friar builds three canticles on one claim: the world hangs together by number and music. Christian Kabbalah, the music of the spheres, and the concord of great world and small man weave through the Latin text.

Giorgi advised princes and churchmen, and his vast synthesis shaped Renaissance thought on architecture, music, and the soul. Later readers mined it for the hidden math of beauty. The book stands as the great Renaissance statement of universal harmony, learned, devout, and bold in its reach.
douglass-narrative-1845:
Frederick Douglass published his Narrative in 1845, seven years after escaping slavery in Maryland. He was still legally a fugitive, so printing his real name and his owners' names took nerve. The book sold fast on both sides of the Atlantic.

Douglass tells of his childhood on plantations, his hunger, and the whippings he saw and suffered. He teaches himself to read, grasping that literacy is a path to freedom. His fight with the slave-breaker Covey marks his turn from submission to resistance. The Narrative remains the most influential American slave narrative ever written. White allies wrote prefaces vouching that the story was truly his.
fremont-report-rocky-mountains-1845:
John Frémont, an army topographer, led surveys to the Rocky Mountains in 1842 and again in 1843 and 1844. His Report, published by Congress in 1845, made him famous as the Pathfinder. His wife Jessie helped shape the narrative, and Kit Carson guided the march.

The report maps the Oregon Trail, South Pass, and the Great Basin, and it describes California's valleys. Settlers used it as a guidebook for the wagon roads west. Frémont's claim that the Basin had no outlet to the sea fixed a key fact of western geography. Few government reports have moved so many people to pack and go.
plos-pone-0003445:
Céline Méhats and co-authors tested a drug class on newborn rat lungs in this 2008 study. Breathing pure oxygen for long harms fragile newborn lungs. It draws in white blood cells and stalls air sac growth. Drugs that block phosphodiesterase 4 are strong anti-inflammatory agents.

The team gave such a drug to newborn rats exposed to high oxygen. They then checked air sac formation, called alveolarization, plus the toxic damage. Lung disorders of early life are a target use for these drugs. The study tests whether blocking this enzyme can protect developing lungs.
plos-pone-0003545:

plos-pone-0009445: Cells behave differently in a flat dish than in the 3D world of real tissue, and this paper digs into why. The authors show that whether fibroblast cells grow on a surface or inside a 3D scaffold changes how their internal skeleton assembles and how they burn energy. The study is a caution to biologists: dish-flat cells may mislead, and the shape of the neighborhood matters.
plos-pone-0009545: Quantitative PCR is the gold standard for measuring DNA — but this paper finds a common calibration method inflates the numbers. Using circular, supercoiled plasmid DNA as the reference standard systematically overestimates quantities. The study is a technical warning: a lab staple may be skewing results across fields that rely on precise DNA counting.
plos-pone-0009645: The stomach bacterium H. pylori varies by region and people. This study maps its genetic and ethnic differentiation within Iran. The paper shows how a global germ fractures into local varieties, shaped by the human populations it lives in — a microbial mirror of human diversity.
plos-pone-0010445: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common soft-tissue cancer in children. This mouse study delivers drugs straight to the tumor by targeting furin, a protein the cancer displays. The paper offers a guided-missile approach to a childhood cancer. The targeted approach could spare children the worst side effects of chemo.
plos-pone-0010545: The enzyme PNGase strips sugars from proteins — but it may have a second job. This study finds evidence for a sugar-removal-independent role in fruit flies. The paper reveals hidden versatility in a housekeeping enzyme. The second job suggests enzymes often moonlight in cells.
plos-pone-0010645: Bird flu H5N1 devastates poultry and threatens people. This study shows one shot of recombinant hemagglutinin protects chickens. The paper offers a simple vaccine for a dangerous virus. The single-dose success could simplify mass poultry vaccination campaigns worldwide.
plos-pone-0010745: Avipoxvirus is killing Hawaii's unique birds. This study builds a Taqman real-time PCR test that finds viral DNA in the blood of Hawaii amakihi. The paper delivers a diagnostic tool. The test helps track and fight the disease in island birds.
plos-pone-0010845: Multiple myeloma, a plasma-cell cancer, still has no cure. This study shows CD137 ligand signaling halts proliferation and triggers suicide in myeloma cell lines. The paper offers a new therapeutic lever. The pathway could be drugged to extend lives. The signal turns the cancer's own switches against it.
plos-pone-0010945: One gene sculpts both eyes and muscles in fish. This study shows the Atoh8 protein is needed to build the retina and body muscle of zebrafish. The paper defines its two jobs. The finding shows how one factor shapes different tissues. The factor works in two worlds at once.
plos-pone-0011045: Quercetin, a compound in many fruits and teas, quiets brain-cell chatter. This study shows it targets a key synaptic protein and weakens signal transmission between neurons. The paper reveals how the supplement acts on the brain. The finding warns that natural pills can alter brain signaling.
plos-pone-0011145: Sepsis rewires the DNA packing of lung defense cells. This study shows a protein called IRAK-M controls how DNA repacks in lung macrophages during sepsis. The paper reveals DNA-level reprogramming. The finding could yield sepsis treatments. The treatments would calm the immune storm.
plos-pone-0011245: Caffeine shields the genome's reading machinery from UV damage. This study shows caffeine prevents transcription shutdown and P-TEFb/7SK dissociation after UV-induced DNA damage. The paper reveals a protective effect. The finding informs DNA-repair research. The protective effect is a bonus of coffee.
plos-pone-0011345: HIV's mutant swarm shifts under drug pressure. This study dissects the dynamics of HIV-1 quasispecies during antiviral treatment using ultra-deep pyrosequencing. The paper reveals viral evolution. The finding aids HIV therapy. The aided therapy anticipates resistance. The anticipated resistance guides drug switches.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1245:
Britain's team tabled this proposal on 24 July 1945. It came from the summit's second week, two days before the election count changed the British leadership. The paper set London's stand on its point in formal words.

By then the talks had moved past first positions. A proposal at this stage was built to be traded against, line by line. This one shows the British hand in that process. It also gains point from its timing. The men who wrote it were about to leave the table. Their successors would own whatever it won or lost.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1345:
Loy Henderson, director of the Office of Near Eastern and African Affairs, wrote to the acting secretary of state on 30 July 1945. Henderson spoke for the State Department's Middle East and Africa desk at the close of the Potsdam talks. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

A bureau chief writing to the acting secretary shows a question rising to the top of the home office. The end of July 1945 brought no rest for regional desks, even as the summit wound down in Germany. Readers get the view from Washington. The problems of the Near East are arriving on the desk of the man running the department while Byrnes was abroad.
frus-1945-50-intel-d45:
Minutes dated 14 November 1945 record another meeting in the long autumn round on intelligence. By then, committees at State, War, and the Budget Bureau had all drafted plans. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Mid-November was the season of sorting: too many plans, one president, and a need to blend them. Meeting minutes from such weeks often hide drama in flat prose, recording outcomes without the argument that produced them. Readers should read these minutes between the papers around them. The memoranda supply the voices; the minutes supply the score. Together they show a government converging, slowly and with friction, on the central system it would announce in January.
frus-1945-50-intel-d145:
Formal minutes cover the Third Meeting of the National Intelligence Authority, held on 2 April 1946. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 145 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

The pages give the meeting in the plain form staff used at the time: a topic, the sense of the talk, and the result. The brevity is the point: what the group did not settle, the minutes do not claim it did. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d245:
A memorandum from the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) reached Secretary of Defense Forrestal on 24 October 1947. It stands as document 245 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. The CIA was only weeks old, having replaced the Central Intelligence Group in September 1947 under the National Security Act.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d345:
Formal minutes cover the 10th Meeting of the National Security Council, held on 22 April 1948. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 345, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The Cold War was turning harder that year, and the new Council and CIA were being tested by it week by week.

Minutes trade color for proof: they may skip the tone of a talk, but they pin down its outcome. Read with the papers before and after it, the record shows a policy taking shape one meeting at a time. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1861-d45:
From London on 17 May 1861, Charles Francis Adams wrote his first report to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 45 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Adams had just reached London, the hardest post in the service. His father and grandfather had both served there before him. His first reports show a calm, exact man taking the measure of Lord John Russell and the British cabinet in a perilous month. His cool head in those first weeks set the tone for seven years of service in London. Cool heads were the rarest goods in London that spring, and Adams had one.
frus-1861-d145:
On 19 August 1861, William H. Seward wrote to William Dayton for the third time in three days. The letter is document 145 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two days after the paired letters, Seward wrote to Paris yet again. The density of the August file shows where his worry lay. France, with its restless emperor, needed the steadiest hand Washington could keep on it. Worry, in Seward's world, was best met with work, and the file shows him working. Work was his answer to worry, and the posts abroad felt the good of it. Worry, for Seward, was best answered with work.
frus-1861-d245:
Writing home was James Shepherd Pike's duty, and his letter of 12 July 1861 went to Seward. Congress received it as Document 245 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d45:
The State Department sent word to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London on 8 April 1862, over Seward's name. Congress received it as Document 45 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the spring of 1862, a year into the war, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d145:
Document 145 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume is a dispatch dated 15 September 1862 from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It belongs to the near-daily mail between the State Department and its most watched post abroad.

Britain was the one power that could change the war by backing the Confederacy, so Adams's post carried great weight. Mail on the London channel bore orders, news of the war, and the Union case against foreign help for the South. Read in sequence, the letters show how Washington worked to keep Britain neutral, week by week, in the fall of 1862.
frus-1862-d245:
William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 11 December 1861, in a letter printed as Document 245 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

December 1861 was the Trent month, when Britain and the Union stood near war over seized Confederate envoys. France's stance mattered because Napoleon III often moved with London on American questions. Dayton's reports from Paris told Washington whether France would back Britain, stay quiet, or use the moment for its own plans in Mexico. Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d345:
Document 345 is the second Seward dispatch to William L. Dayton dated 10 November 1862, printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Secretary of State William H. Seward sent both letters to Paris in one mail.

Paired letters late in the year carry a different mood from September's: the questions are the same, but the urgency has ebbed. France, left alone by Britain, chose to send its truce idea to Washington and Richmond directly, where it failed. This letter belongs to the quieter work of watching that failure unfold. Seward paired Dayton's reports with Mercier's remarks in Washington to test each against the other.
frus-1862-d445:
Norman B. Judd, the American minister in Berlin, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 December 1861. It is Document 445 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, among the first Prussian papers in the volume.

Judd wrote in the month of the Trent crisis, when war with Britain seemed possible and every European court's attitude counted double. From Berlin he could report how Prussia and the smaller German states read the American conflict. Prussian sympathy leaned to the Union, and German volunteers were crossing the Atlantic to enlist. His early report helped Seward map the friendly ground in Europe at the end of the war's first year.
frus-1862-d545:
On 10 September 1862 Roest van Limburg sent this note to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as Document 545 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, accompanying the President's annual message.

Van Limburg wrote in the week between Lee's invasion of Maryland and the battle of Antietam, when every legation in Washington was waiting. His own business was the durable Dutch agenda of commerce and neutral right, which did not pause for campaigns. The note is one of the September pieces of the Netherlands file. It was framed in Washington. Meanwhile its writer's colleagues abroad, Pike among them, reported the same crisis from the other side of the ocean. The two Dutch files together give the volume's most balanced small-power record.
frus-1862-d645:
Townsend Harris, the first American minister to Japan, wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 2 December 1861. Harris had opened the American legation in Japan only a few years before, after long talks led to a trade treaty in 1858. His letter is document 645 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Reports like this one carried word from a distant post back to Washington. Harris wrote about the state of ties with Japan's rulers and the day-to-day work of a small legation far from home. Read now, the letter shows how the United States kept a foothold in Japan while the Civil War raged back home.
frus-1863p1-d45:
Judah P. Benjamin wrote this letter to James M. Mason on 26 September 1862. Benjamin was the Confederate secretary of state; Mason was the South's envoy in London. The letter is document 45 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Mason and Slidell were the twin heads of the South's push in Europe, one in London and one in Paris. Benjamin wrote to both in the same week of September 1862. His letters fed them the South's case at the moment its armies stood near their peak. This one, printed in the Union's own volume, lets a reader weigh that case in the words of the man who made it.
frus-1863p1-d145:
A lone sheet between clusters, this dispatch from Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward is dated 7 April 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 145 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Adams wrote days after the British seized a Southern-built raider at Liverpool, a win the Union had sought for months. His mail that week told Washington how the act was taken in London. It is a lone sheet between clusters, and it catches the file at a turn. The ship fight, long a dread, had begun to break the Union's way. The calm tone is Adams's own.
frus-1863p1-d245:
The State Department's mail for London dated 23 July 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 245 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Union victories in July 1863 let Washington speak with more confidence. Orders sent after Gettysburg and Vicksburg carry a firmer note than those of the spring. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d345:
A note dated 29 December 1862 carried the British position from Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 345 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

London watched for any sign that Washington meant to widen the war. Lyons's job was to read American intentions and report them home faithfully. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d445:
On 4 April 1863 a formal note passed from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d545:
Secretary of State William H. Seward received a letter dated 30 May 1863 from Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d645:
A 23 October 1863 dispatch from Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London reached William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

From the London end, the work was pressure and reporting. Adams pushed the British government on Confederate shipbuilding and sent home his reading of British politics and opinion. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
plos-pbio-0020045:
Rony Paz and Eilon Vaadia measured how practice sharpens brain signals in PLOS Biology in 2004. Their focus was the primary motor cortex, the strip that helps plan and send movement commands. Monkeys learned to move in specific directions while the team read the firing of single neurons.

After learning, those neurons coded movement direction more clearly. Both writing the signal and reading it back improved. That is direct proof that practice refines the code itself, not just the muscles. The result matters for understanding skill learning of all kinds. It also bears on brain-based prosthetics, which rely on reading motor signals as cleanly as possible.
plos-pbio-0020245:
Amit Gur and Dani Zamir made a case for wild plant genes in PLOS Biology in 2004. Crop plants were bred for yield so long that much natural variation was left behind. The authors argue that wild kin of crops still hold unused variants that can lift yields past current limits.

Breeders often find that adding one wild variant helps, then gains stall. Gur and Zamir show the stall is not the end: the right mix of wild segments can push past it. Their case rests on tomato work, where wild relatives are a rich store. The message for food security is plain. Gene banks and wild stands are not museums; they are working tools for future harvests.
plos-pone-0000145:
Eun Sung Park, Ju-Seog Lee, Hyun Goo Woo, and colleagues published this breast cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cancer outcomes vary widely between patients, partly because genes in the tumor affect the odds of invasion and spread. The authors test whether a gene expression signature from tissue culture can predict a patient's prognosis.

The pattern of genes switched on in a tumor, they argue, can reflect how that cancer will behave. The paper checks a signature grown outside the body against real human breast cancer outcomes. If such signatures hold up, doctors could sort patients by risk earlier and match treatment to the likely course.
plos-pone-0000245:
Brian A. Coll, Rafael A. Garcia, and William N. Marmer published this food safety paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Government feed bans left meat and bone meal with few legal uses. New uses need its protein to be soluble and free of the prion that causes BSE, mad cow disease. The authors study how protease enzymes diffuse into the meal to improve solubility and possibly inactivate the prion.

An enzyme that can only treat the surface of a particle is of little use. Measuring how far protease soaks in tells whether the treatment can work at scale. The paper addresses both a waste problem and a safety problem left behind by the BSE crisis.
plos-pone-0000345:
David Dingli, Arne Traulsen, and Jorge M. Pacheco published this theoretical hematology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hematopoiesis, the making of blood, runs through compartments of stem and maturing cells in the bone marrow. The authors model the architecture and dynamics of those compartments, how cells flow from stem cells to the many blood cell types.

A compartment model turns marrow organization into numbers that can be tested. It helps explain how blood production stays stable and what happens when it fails or turns cancerous. The framework is used in studying leukemia, where the compartment structure is distorted.
plos-pone-0000445:
Paul Smolen built a computer model of how memories become long-lasting, described in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Late long-term potentiation is the lasting strengthening of a synapse, the connection between neurons, hours after learning. Smolen's model simulates aspects of memory maintenance, the processes that keep that strengthening from fading.

A model must choose which molecules and feedback loops matter, then check whether the simulated synapse behaves like a real one. Getting maintenance right is the hard part of memory theory, since memories outlive the molecules that formed them. Simulations like this help biologists decide which experiments will best test how memories endure.
plos-pone-0000545:
Zoltán Oláh and colleagues found that several pain drugs block a key pain channel, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The channel is TRPV1, the heat and chili-pepper sensor on pain neurons, a prime target for new analgesics. Anti-calmodulins and tricyclic adjuvants used in pain therapy blocked the TRPV1 channel in their tests.

Tricyclic drugs are prescribed for chronic pain for reasons that were never fully clear. If part of their action is blocking TRPV1, an old drug gains a modern mechanism. Knowing the target also suggests designing cleaner blockers that keep the benefit without the tricyclics' broad side effects.
plos-pone-0000645:
Viviane Villard, George W. Agak, Géraldine Frank and colleagues hunted for malaria vaccine candidates using a shape clue, in PLOS ONE in 2007. They focused on alpha-helical coiled coils, protein segments twisted like ropes. The chosen segments came from proteins expected in the parasite's blood stage, the phase that makes people sick.

Synthetic copies of those segments should mimic the real parasite structures that antibodies target. The team reports making 95 such chemical candidates for screening. A fast route to promising antigens matters because malaria vaccine work has been slow and hard. Their motif-based shortcut aims to hand vaccine developers a ready shortlist.
plos-pone-0000745:
Jeffrey L. Froula and M. Pilar Francino found that bacteria purge fake gene-start signals, and that the purge tracks protein output. RNA polymerase, the enzyme that copies genes, can bind misplaced DNA sites and waste effort. Selection for efficient gene expression should therefore control where polymerase-binding motifs appear across the genome. The authors analyze the distribution of those motifs.

Their title states the pattern: selection against spurious promoter motifs correlates with translational efficiency across bacteria. In plain terms, genomes are proofread by evolution against costly distractions. The cleaner the genome, the better its genes seem to translate. It is a tidy link between genome hygiene and growth economics.
plos-pone-0000845:
Imad J. Matouk and colleagues argued that an RNA which makes no protein is essential for human tumor growth, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Mutations and aberrant growth factor signaling contribute to carcinogenesis. Recent studies had revealed that non-coding RNAs are controllers of gene expression. H19 is an imprinted gene, expressed only from the mother's copy, and it produces an RNA without a protein product.

Their title states the strong claim: the H19 non-coding RNA is essential for human tumor growth. Essential means tumors fail without it, making it a candidate drug target despite encoding nothing. Non-coding RNAs were then rising from genomic curiosities to central cancer players.
plos-pone-0000945:
Zach Klapholz-Brown, Graham Walmsley, Ysbrand Nusse and colleagues read the gene program Wnt protein triggers in human fibroblasts, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Wnt signaling guides development, stem cell renewal and tissue shape, and it plays a part in cancer. Fibroblasts are the support cells that build the tissue around other cells.

By switching Wnt on in these cells and reading which genes answer, the team sketch how tissues set their local character. Their results suggest mechanisms for cell cooperativity, cells working together to define their shared space. The work links a famous signal to the quiet background cells that make organs hold together.
plos-pone-0001045:
Alassane Dicko, David Diemert, Issaka Sagara and colleagues measured antibody responses to a malaria vaccine in Malian adults, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The vaccine targeted AMA1, a protein on the malaria parasite's invading form. AMA1 is a leading blood stage vaccine candidate, and in monkeys protection tracked with antibody levels.

Adults in Mali, where malaria is common, joined a randomized, double blind phase one trial. Testing there matters because prior exposure shapes responses in ways clean lab populations cannot show. The team report the vaccine's impact on antibody responses. Early safety and response data decide whether a candidate moves toward trials in children.
plos-pone-0001145:
Phages, the viruses that infect bacteria, might one day help treat infections that antibiotics no longer cure. Aušra Gaidelytė, Martti Vaara, and Dennis Bamford surveyed phages in the most severe kind of bacterial infection, septicemia, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. How phage ecology plays out during such infections was obscure.

The authors examined which phages are present in blood infection cases and how they relate to the bacteria involved. Using phages as therapy is attractive against drug-resistant bacteria, but it depends on this ecology. Their survey gives an early map of the phage landscape in septicemia.
plos-pone-0001245:
As organisms grow, their body shapes change in patterned ways, a subject called ontogenetic allometry. Hongying Li, Zhongwen Huang, and Junyi Gai note that almost nothing is known about the genes behind those changes, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. One reason is the lack of a conceptual framework for mapping them.

The authors propose such a framework for mapping quantitative trait loci, genome regions affecting measurable traits, that regulate how allometry unfolds over development. Their model treats growth as a process to be mapped, not just a final size. It opens a route to the genetics of shape change.
plos-pone-0001345:
North American monarch butterflies migrate spectacularly each fall, while summer generations stay and breed. Haisun Zhu, Amy Casselman, and Steven Reppert built a genetic resource for studying that difference, in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. Migrants are deficient in juvenile hormone, which leads to reproductive diapause and increased longevity, and they navigate using a time-compensated sun compass.

The authors present a brain expressed sequence tag resource for summer and migratory monarchs: a catalogue of genes active in the brain of each type. Comparing the two catalogues hunts for migration genes. The resource serves any group studying how one genome produces two such different butterflies.
plos-pone-0001445:
Alfred Banda and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on HIV drug care in the Malawi Defence Force. HIV hits all parts of society, and armed forces are no exception. The team ran a national survey of all sites in Malawi that give HIV drugs. They asked how many soldiers got care, how they fared, and how death rates changed.

Their survey gives the first full count for this group in the country. It shows both gains and gaps in access to life saving drugs. Armies need fit troops, so such data guide force health plans. The work also adds to the record of how free drug roll out played out in Malawi.
plos-pone-0001545:
Toby Knowles and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on leg ills in meat chickens. In fifty years, breeding pushed chicken growth from 25 grams a day to 100. That speed has a cost, as many birds limp or fail to walk well. The team surveyed how common leg ills are and what drives them.

Their survey weighs farm traits against leg health bird by bird. It also tests steps that could cut the burden. Fast growth and leg pain pose a clear welfare clash. Hard counts give farmers and rule makers a base for change that loose concern cannot.
plos-pone-0001645:
Valériane Leroy, Didier K. Ekouevi, Renaud Becquet, and their co-authors reported an 18-month study from Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire, on stopping HIV from passing from mothers to babies. Their 2008 PLOS ONE research article covers short courses of antiretroviral drugs given around birth. The women also used options other than long breastfeeding, which can carry the virus to the child.

The team checked how well this combined plan worked over the first year and a half of the children's lives. The full text gives the drug schedules, the feeding choices, and the infection rates in the babies. Short drug courses plus safer feeding were a key strategy where long-term treatment could not be supplied. Real-world results like these guided care for mothers with HIV.
plos-pone-0001745:
Paulo R. Guimarães, Mauro Galetti, and Pedro Jordano rethought fruits built for giant animals that no longer exist, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Some South American fleshy fruits match fruits in the paleotropics that are spread by megafauna, mammals over a thousand kilograms. Those giants went extinct in South America 10,000 to 15,000 years ago, yet the plants persist.

Such seed dispersal anachronisms are best explained by past interactions with extinct giants. The authors ask what spreads these fruits now and what the mismatch means. The full text gives the fruit and animal comparisons across continents. The work warns that some plants are ecological ghosts, still shaped by partners lost thousands of years ago.
plos-pone-0001845:
Stéphane Caut, Elodie Guirlet, Elena Angulo, and their co-authors traced Atlantic leatherback turtle feeding areas with isotope analysis in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The leatherback has declined dramatically over 25 years, mainly from deaths in fishing gear, plus harvest of eggs and nesting females. Atlantic leatherbacks undertake long migrations between nesting beaches and feeding grounds.

Isotope signatures in turtle tissues record where they fed. The team's analysis reveals a foraging area dichotomy: two distinct feeding strategies or grounds among the turtles. The full text gives the isotope data and the inferred regions. Knowing where turtles feed tells conservationists which fisheries must change gear to save them.
plos-pone-0001945:
Ryosuke Kawakami and co-authors studied left and right in the brains of mutant mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In higher animals, the two sides of the brain are not mirror copies; each side favors some tasks. Yet the genes and cell steps that set up that split were unclear.

The team worked with mice whose inner organs sit on the reversed side, a mutant called inversus viscerum. They had found that the hippocampus, a memory area, wires itself in a left-right pattern tied to how NMDA receptor parts are dealt out. The study asks whether the brain of these mutants shows a right-side pattern on both sides.
plos-pone-0002045:
Daniel Keller and co-authors modeled how a key learning protein switches on in tiny nerve knobs, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. When calcium enters a dendritic spine, it sets off a chain of reactions. The chain starts with the activation of calmodulin and ends with lasting changes in synapse strength. That chain underlies learning and memory at the cell level.

How fully calmodulin switches on depends on sharp local spikes in calcium inside the small spine. The team modeled those spikes and the protein's response in the crowded spine head. The work links the brief physics of a calcium pulse to lasting brain change.
plos-pone-0002145:
Marcos Antezana and King Jordan studied how mutation patterns differ along the chromosomes of warm-blooded animals, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Hans Egede, a Norwegian pastor, sailed to Greenland in 1721 to renew its old Norse church. His Description of Greenland reached English readers in 1745. Egede wrote from long years on that coast, reporting its ice, animals, and Inuit people for a Europe that knew almost nothing of them.
